confirmed.title: L402 and card rail references come from the agent and are never tied to the challenge the signer pays, so a paid transaction can be released and the budget reused
confirmed.description: For l402 and card-psp, the ledger's rail_reference is `binding.railReference`, which is `o.railReference` (bindSignedOffer, line 111). That value is a free field in the agent's PaymentOption. Nothing checks that it matches the challenge the gateway signs over (challengeDigest) and the signer actually pays: the L402 invoice paymentHash, or the card challenge.id. Reconciliation (reconcileOne, lines 289-295) asks the rail about rail_reference only, and it releases the row when the rail says 'not paid' after the authorization has expired. So the 'release only with proof the payment cannot happen' rule can be satisfied by proof about a different invoice or intent. On the card path the signer also never compares intent.resource with auth.resource (cardPsp.ts createCardPayment), so an intent for another resource of the same merchant at the same price is paid as well.
confirmed.failureScenario: Reproduced in a throwaway worktree at e4b6da3. Setup: SAT mandate with totalLimit 25 and maxPerTransaction 25, authorizationTtlSeconds 2. The agent fetches Spree's 402 twice and gets invoices I1 and I2. It sends /authorize with option = the I1 challenge but railReference = I2.paymentHash, and the gateway authorizes. The signer pays I1, and the seller is credited 25 sat. The agent reports outcome 'payment_failed'. After 2 s, /reconcile looks up I2 (unpaid), and the transaction becomes 'released' with committed back to 0. Repeating this three times gave the seller 75 sat against a 25 sat mandate, and the budget still showed 25 available. The card path does the same with challenge.id=pi_A (confirmed) and railReference=pi_B (never confirmed).
confirmed.suggestedFix: Have the gateway derive the rail reference from the challenge it binds instead of trusting option.railReference. For L402, decode challenge.invoice and use its paymentHash; also check that its amount and payee equal the offer price. For card, use challenge.id, fetch the intent from the PSP and check its amount, currency, merchant and resource against the offer. Reject the request if option.railReference differs. In createCardPayment, also require intent.resource === auth.resource.
notes: I read the code at e4b6da3 and it confirms the finding. The gateway's rail_reference for l402 and card-psp is the railReference field the agent supplies. The gateway never checks that value against the challenge it signs over. The signer checks only challengeDigest, then pays challenge.invoice (or challenge.id). confirmed.title: x402 network, asset and EIP-712 domain in the challenge are not bound to the signed offer or the authorization; the signer signs whatever token and chain the challenge names
confirmed.description: The gateway compares only the agent's option fields (amount, currency, payTo, resource) with the signed offer price. option.currency itself comes from the challenge's `extra.name` label (parseX402), not from the asset. The challenge object the signer uses goes into the authorization only as an opaque digest. createX402Payment checks only req.amount and req.payTo against the authorization. It then builds the EIP-712 domain from req.network, req.asset and req.extra, none of which the gateway or the signer compares with the offer's PriceOption.network and asset. CHAIN_IDS includes Base mainnet (8453). So an approved seller (or anyone shaping the challenge) can get a TransferWithAuthorization signed for a different token contract or a different chain at the same atomic amount. Examples: mainnet USDC instead of Sepolia test USDC, a 6-decimal token worth more, or a token whose name is spoofed as 'USDC'. The user's mandate in USDC and the 'amount must equal the signed price' rule are then met only in name.
confirmed.failureScenario: Reproduced: from Spree's real 402, keep amount 20000 and payTo, and set requirements.network='eip155:8453', asset='0x…0bad', extra.name='USDC'. Gateway /authorize returned 200 (authorized). Signer /pay returned 200 with a PAYMENT-SIGNATURE whose accepted.network is eip155:8453 and accepted.asset is 0x…0bad. That is a valid EIP-3009 authorization for a chain and token the user never approved, which the seller can submit there.
confirmed.suggestedFix: In bindSignedOffer, for x402, read the challenge's requirements and require network, asset (getAddress-normalised), amount, payTo and scheme 'exact' to equal the offer's PriceOption. Derive currency from a pinned asset→currency table, not extra.name. Put network and asset into PaymentAuthorization, and have createX402Payment refuse a requirements object whose network or asset differ from the authorization, or whose extra (domain name and version) is not the pinned one for that asset.

confirmed.title: Agent identity is self-asserted and payment credentials are handed to any caller: unauthenticated GET /transactions/:id exposes the signed authorization, and the signer replays the credential to whoever presents it
confirmed.description: The gateway's assignee checks (authorize, outcome, reconcile) compare a plain `agentId` string from the request body; nothing authenticates it. GET /transactions/:id needs no agentId at all and returns auth_json, the full gateway-signed authorization. The exact challenge is written to the Pod evidence (sc:challenge). The signer's /pay pays or replays for anyone holding authorization plus challenge (`done.get(authId)` returns the stored credential). So any local process can obtain another agent's live payment credential: the x402 PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, the L402 macaroon:preimage, or the card Payment header. It can also authorize spending under any agent's name. The README says a different agent 'cannot spend: it is not an assignee of the mandate', but that holds only if agents don't lie about their id. The design's threat table does not list this.
confirmed.failureScenario: Agent 1 buys a POST (non-repeatable) paid route. A second process reads GET {gateway}/transactions/{txId} (no auth) to get auth_json, reads the challenge from {pod}/transactions/{txId}.ttl, and POSTs both to {signer}/pay. It gets the same credential back (replayed:true) and presents it to the proxy first. That consumes the one delivery the user paid for, and agent 1 gets 402 credential_consumed. For GET routes the credential gives the thief unlimited free re-delivery. The same process can also call /authorize with agentId=AGENT_1 against AGENT_1's mandate.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Authenticate callers of the gateway and signer, for example with per-agent keys, mTLS or a signed request bound to agentId. Bind the authorization to the requesting agent's key, and have the signer return a credential only to that key. Require the same check on GET /transactions/:id, or remove auth_json from the response. Until then, state in README and design.md that agent identity is not authenticated and that the assignee check assumes honest agents.

confirmed.title: Superseded mandate/meaning revisions stay valid: an agent with Pod write access can roll back to an older signed revision
confirmed.description: When the user revises a record, commit() copies the previous revision byte for byte into history/<slug>-rN.ttl. That copy keeps status UserConfirmed, the original subject IRI and a valid signature. The 'Superseded' status is declared in model.ts but nothing ever uses it. verifyConfirmation (approval.ts), the gateway's loadMandate (gatewayService.ts:81-91) and CommonGround.load only check that the signature matches the record's terms. None of them checks that the revision is the latest one the user signed, and no revocation or high-water mark exists anywhere. The signature covers id and revision, but the id is the same in every revision. So an older revision copied back over the live document verifies cleanly. The ledger keys the budget by mandate id, so the restored higher limit applies to the same running total. The same trick works for agreed meanings and requirements (for example restoring 'current = 60 min' after the user tightened it to 15). Grounded requirements then follow it through effectiveCriterion. The threat model in docs/design.md says 'Agent or anyone with Pod write access raises a limit -> Mandate signature no longer verifies', but this route raises the limit and the signature still verifies.
confirmed.failureScenario: Reproduced in-process. The device signs mandate r1 (totalLimit 1 USDC, maxPerTransaction 1). The user then signs r2 (totalLimit 0.10, maxPerTransaction 0.05, supersedes history/...-r1.ttl), and commit() archives the r1 bytes. An agent copies history/weatherreport-usdc-r1.ttl over mandates/weatherreport-usdc.ttl. parseRecord(ttl1, mandateId) followed by verifyConfirmation returns { ok: true } with totalLimit '1'. The gateway's loadMandate does only this, so /authorize then allows up to 1 USDC in total and 1 USDC per purchase again, although the user cut the limit to 0.10 / 0.05.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Make the newest revision binding. Options: write archived revisions with status Superseded and keep a per-record minimum revision (or the digest of the current signed revision) somewhere agents cannot write, such as the gateway's ledger, a user-signed revision index, or the device. Then make the gateway and CommonGround.load reject any revision below it. At minimum, the gateway should remember the highest revision it has seen per mandate id and refuse anything lower. Add an e2e regression test that copies the history document back.

confirmed.title: Existing mandate is reused when the user asks for narrower terms; the narrower per-purchase limit, expiry and other terms are silently dropped
confirmed.description: negotiate() reuses an existing confirmed mandate whenever its totalLimit and currency equal the new request and it has not expired. It ignores maxPerTransaction, validUntil/validDays, assignees and allowedSellers. The assistant reports 'Existing mandate covers this request; no new spending authority requested', but the mandate it reuses can allow more than the user just stated. The user's latest statement of what may be spent is never shown on the approval device and never recorded, so the agent keeps acting on broader authority than the user currently means.
confirmed.failureScenario: Reproduced. A confirmed mandate exists for WeatherReport/USDC with totalLimit 1 and maxPerTransaction 1. The user says 'Get me a Berlin weather report. You may spend up to 1 USDC, at most 0.01 USDC per purchase, from approved providers.' The rule interpreter produces { totalLimit: '1', maxPerTransaction: '0.01' }. negotiate() returns proposals: [] and reuses the old mandate, so a single purchase of up to 1 USDC is authorised without the user seeing anything. The same happens for 'for the next 2 days' (validDays) and for a smaller set of agents.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Build the candidate mandate as now and reuse the existing one only when it is no broader in any term: maxPerTransaction <= requested, validUntil <= requested, assignees and sellers a subset of those requested, schemes a subset. Otherwise propose a new revision for the user to approve. Simplest: reuse only when every authority term is equal.

confirmed.title: Terminal approval device signs an agreed meaning without showing its executable criterion
confirmed.description: summarize() describes a meaning only as its free-text definition ('AGREED MEANING "current" for WeatherReport: <definition>'). The interactive terminal demo (src/demo/run-demo.ts:58-62 and 87) shows the user just the option label and this summary. The signature covers the criterion, which is what ranking and delivery checks actually run. Label, definition and criterion all come from the interpreter's candidate, and with LLM_PROVIDER set that is LLM output. Nothing checks that they agree. A misreading or prompt-injected model can therefore get the user to sign a meaning whose criterion differs from the words shown. The meaning is then reused across sessions and agents without being asked again. The web phone card does show the criterion (approvals.ts describe()), so this affects the terminal device and the canonical summary text.
confirmed.failureScenario: LLM_PROVIDER=openai npm run demo:interactive. The grounded requirement's line does print 'lteq 600', but the meaning can be approved on its own and stays reusable.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Include the criterion (leftOperand, operator, rightOperand, unit) in summarize() for meanings, as the phone card already does. Consider also checking LLM candidates for consistency, for example by rendering each label from its criterion instead of trusting model text.

confirmed.title: Vocabulary validation can be bypassed: criteria in statements with no category are never checked, and a quote in a value defeats the 'skip invalid statement' match
confirmed.description: checkCriterion checks leftOperand only when the statement has its own category. negotiate() then fills in the category from the intention, so a criterion with an unknown property passes. Separately, negotiate() (commonGround.ts:69) finds the invalid statements by applying the greedy regex /"(.*)"/ to each error message. If the offending value contains a double quote (leftOperand is a free string in the LLM schema), the captured text is not the statement text, and the statement flagged invalid is still turned into a proposal. Both break the documented guarantee that anything outside the vocabulary is rejected before proposal. The user still has to approve the result, so this does not create authority by itself.

confirmed.title: 'Verified' rehearsal saves a weather run that did not go as scripted
confirmed.description: README says `--rehearse` "records a verified fallback". docs/demo.md says the rehearsal "stops with an error, and saves nothing, if any step did not go as scripted" and that "a broken run never becomes your fallback". rehearsalProblems() only looks for `error` events, guard cards with tone `fail`, the shoes purchase status and a 'no order yet' note. It never checks the weather scenario. A weather step that returns false (no mandate approved, purchase blocked with no transactionId) stops autoplay without emitting an error. A purchase that ends `completed_noncompliant` or `paid_not_delivered` counts as 'done' and is not checked at all. The guard checks are also weaker than the presenter script says: tamper and unapproved pass on any 403 whatever the code, and replay never checks that Spree really delivered three times (only that Havel returned 402 and the rail shows one transfer).

A presenter replaying it on stage would show a failed delivery as the headline flow.
confirmed.suggestedFix: In rehearsalProblems, flag any `step` event with state 'failed', a weather `purchase` whose status is not 'completed', and a weather `delivery` whose status is not 'Delivered'. Make the tamper and unapproved cards check the expected codes (MANDATE_NOT_CONFIRMED, SELLER_NOT_IN_MANDATE), and make replay require Spree to return 200 three times. Or narrow the docs to the conditions actually checked.

The second sees 'returned', which is neither shipped nor delivered, so line 189 sets it to 'refunded'. On e4b6da3 the order events end [created, shipped, delivered, returned, refunded] and trackOrder gives orderStatus=refunded, delivery.status=Cancelled, so the NonCompliant verdict is replaced. The PSP idempotency key refund:<order> means money is refunded only once (merchant balance 0); only the order status and verdict are wrong. A fix would be an in-flight per-order promise, like `completing` for checkout, or setting status from a snapshot taken before the await.

Minor, found by reading the code and not run: two concurrent buyer cancels of a 'created' order without an Idempotency-Key both reach refund() (acpMerchant.ts:226-235) before o.refund is set. Each pushes an event, so the order gets duplicate 'refunded' events. The final status is still 'refunded', so this is only cosmetic.
